problem_statement: The uIP address library must parse and print IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address using the well-known NAT64 prefix 64:ff9b::/96 and the RFC 4291 mixed dotted-decimal notation (e.g. 64:ff9b::8.8.8.8, ::FFFF:10.0.0.1), and provide the uip_nat64addr helper macro.

verification.reason: The core hidden unit test is fair once the public interface and exact parse/print behaviour of the mixed NAT64/IPv4-mapped forms are specified; the gaps can be repaired without dictating the implementation.

problems.detail: The statement names uip_nat64addr but does not give its exact interface (a uip_ip6addr_t pointer plus four IPv4 octets) or that it must be available through net/ipv6/ip64-addr.h, which the hidden unit test relies on.

The statement gives example mixed notation but not the exact printed forms that the tests compare: IPv4-mapped addresses must print as ::FFFF:a.b.c.d and well-known NAT64 addresses as 64:ff9b::a.b.c.d.

The hidden unit test checks additional mixed-notation cases (full seven-hextet-plus-dotted form, bracketed form, and rejection of malformed input) that are not explicitly covered by the two examples in the statement.

problem_statement_fixed:
The uIP address library must parse and print IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address using the well-known NAT64 prefix 64:ff9b::/96 and the RFC 4291 mixed dotted-decimal notation (e.g. 64:ff9b::8.8.8.8, ::FFFF:10.0.0.1), and provide the uip_nat64addr helper macro.

The parser (uiplib_ip6addrconv) must accept the standard IPv6 forms (including the :: compression and the [bracket] form) as well as the RFC 4291 mixed notation, including the full form of up to seven 16-bit hex groups followed by a dotted-decimal IPv4 suffix (e.g. 2001:db8:1:2:3:4:192.168.1.1). It must return a nonzero value on a successfully parsed address and 0 for malformed or unsupported input (empty strings, non-address text, or too many groups). The printer (uiplib_ipaddr_snprint) must emit NAT64 and IPv4-mapped addresses in the compressed mixed dotted-decimal form (e.g. 64:ff9b::8.8.8.8 and ::FFFF:10.1.2.3) rather than expanding them to full hexadecimal.

The uip_nat64addr macro takes a pointer to a uip_ip6addr_t and four IPv4 octets and sets the address to the NAT64 well-known-prefix form: 64:ff9b::/96 (RFC 6052) with the given IPv4 address placed in the low 32 bits, so that, for example, uip_nat64addr(&addr, 8, 8, 8, 8) yields the address 64:ff9b::8.8.8.8 and uip_nat64addr(&addr, 192, 0, 2, 1) yields 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1.
